title: A Coat, a Reader, and a Cut

scenes.tts: Clathrin is a protein shaped like a three-legged pinwheel. Many copies lock together into a curved cage on the inner face of the membrane. Yet clathrin touches neither the membrane nor the cargo. So what does?
scenes.visual: One three-legged pinwheel turns; copies lock into a curved cage below a membrane with one receptor; red crossed gaps to the membrane and to the receptor tail; a question box between.
scenes.narration: Clathrin is a protein shaped like a three-legged pinwheel. Many copies lock together into a curved cage on the inner face of the membrane. Yet clathrin touches neither the membrane nor the cargo. So what does?

scenes.tts: Adaptor proteins do. The main adaptor at the plasma membrane is A P 2. It holds the lipid P I P 2, a short sequence in a receptor tail, and clathrin. So a receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read.
scenes.caption: Adaptor proteins do. The main adaptor at the plasma membrane is AP2. It holds the lipid PIP2, a short sequence in a receptor tail, and clathrin. So a receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read.
scenes.visual: The same scene; an AP2 block appears and reaches three grips: the PIP2 lipid in the membrane, the sequence on the tail tip, and the clathrin cage. The label says the adaptor reads the tail.
scenes.narration: Adaptor proteins do. The main adaptor at the plasma membrane is AP2. It holds the lipid PIP2, a short sequence in a receptor tail, and clathrin. So a receptor enters a pit because its tail carries a sequence that an adaptor can read.

scenes.tts: Brown and Goldstein met the proof in a patient known as J D. This patient's L D L receptors could bind L D L. But they stayed scattered over the surface instead of gathering in pits, and the cells could not take L D L in. The fault was later traced to one tyrosine in the receptor's tail, replaced by cysteine.
scenes.caption: Brown and Goldstein met the proof in a patient known as J.D. This patient's LDL receptors could bind LDL. But they stayed scattered over the surface instead of gathering in pits, and the cells could not take LDL in. The fault was later traced to one tyrosine in the receptor's tail, replaced by cysteine.
scenes.visual: Names appear; receptors across a membrane strip each hold an LDL particle; they stay spread out while a dashed empty pit with a crossed arrow shows no gathering and no uptake; one tail is shown large and its tyrosine chip is swapped for cysteine.
scenes.narration: Brown and Goldstein met the proof in a patient known as J.D. This patient's LDL receptors could bind LDL. scenes.tts: A pit deepens until it hangs from the surface by a thin neck. Dynamin, a large G T Pase, assembles into a collar around the neck. When it hydrolyzes G T P, the neck is cut. The coat is then stripped off, and the bare vesicle can fuse with its target.
scenes.caption: A pit deepens until it hangs from the surface by a thin neck. Dynamin, a large GTPase, assembles into a collar around the neck. When it hydrolyzes GTP, the neck is cut. The coat is then stripped off, and the bare vesicle can fuse with its target.
scenes.visual: A coated pit deepens to a flask on a thin neck; dynamin pieces gather and close into a collar; a GTP chip flashes and the neck is cut; the coat pieces lift away and the bare vesicle moves to a target membrane.
scenes.narration: A pit deepens until it hangs from the surface by a thin neck. Dynamin, a large GTPase, assembles into a collar around the neck. When it hydrolyzes GTP, the neck is cut. The coat is then stripped off, and the bare vesicle can fuse with its target.
